metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Companion for GCP Compute Services - covers Compute Engine, App Engine, Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, instance groups, autoscaling, preemptible/spot VMs, and GPUs/TPUs.

questions.title: Compute Engine Overview
questions.scenario: A company is migrating their on-premises virtual machine workloads to GCP. They need full control over the operating system and installed software.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides virtual machines with full control over the OS?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which GCP service model gives you the most control over the underlying infrastructure, similar to managing your own data center?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Compute Engine is GCP's IaaS platform that provides virtual machines running on Google's global infrastructure. You get full control over the operating system, can install any software, configure networking, and manage the VM exactly like a physical server. App Engine (A) is PaaS with managed runtimes, Cloud Run (B) runs containers serverlessly, and Cloud Functions (C) is event-driven FaaS. For lift-and-shift migrations requiring OS-level control, Compute Engine is the clear choice.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Compute Engine offers predefined machine types (E2, N2, N2D, C3, M3, A2, G2) as well as custom machine types where you specify exact vCPU and memory configurations to avoid over-provisioning.
  • Supports Windows Server, multiple Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS, RHEL, SLES), and fully custom images imported from on-premises or other clouds via the image import tool.
  • Provides sole-tenant nodes for compliance requirements mandating physical isolation, and Shielded VMs for verified boot integrity against rootkits and boot-level malware.
  • Live migration transparently moves running VMs between physical hosts during maintenance events, achieving near-zero downtime without any action from the user.

questions.title: Machine Type Selection
questions.scenario: A data science team needs VMs with high memory-to-CPU ratio for running in-memory analytics workloads.
questions.questionText: Which Compute Engine machine type family should they choose?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider which machine type family is specifically designed to provide the highest ratio of memory to virtual CPUs, targeting workloads like in-memory databases and large-scale analytics.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Memory-optimized (M series) machine types deliver the highest memory-to-vCPU ratios on GCP, with configurations supporting up to 12 TB of RAM. They are purpose-built for in-memory databases like SAP HANA, Redis clusters, and in-memory analytics engines. Accelerator-optimized A2 (A) is built around NVIDIA A100 GPUs for ML training, not memory-heavy analytics. Compute-optimized C series (B) maximizes per-core performance for CPU-bound workloads like gaming servers and HPC. General-purpose E2/N2 (C) offers a balanced ratio suitable for most workloads but lacks the extreme memory density needed here.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The M series includes M1 (up to 4 TB RAM), M2 (up to 12 TB RAM), and M3 generations, each offering progressively better price-performance for memory-intensive workloads like SAP HANA and large-scale analytics.
  • M3 machine types provide the latest generation with improved memory bandwidth and are the recommended choice for new deployments; M1/M2 remain available for existing workloads.
  • Compute-optimized C3 machines offer the highest per-core performance with Intel Sapphire Rapids processors, ideal for gaming, HPC, and single-threaded applications, but not high memory ratios.
  • For workloads needing more memory than general-purpose types but less than M series, consider custom machine types with extended memory, which allow up to 8 GB per vCPU at additional cost.

questions.title: Custom Machine Types
questions.scenario: Your application requires 6 vCPUs and 24 GB of memory, but no predefined machine type matches this configuration exactly.
questions.questionText: How can you create a VM with this exact configuration?

choices.text: Custom configurations are not supported in Compute Engine
Create a custom machine type with the specific vCPU and memory values
Deploy two smaller VMs and load balance between them
Use the closest predefined machine type and ignore the extra resources

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Compute Engine allows you to define your own machine type by specifying the exact number of vCPUs and amount of memory, avoiding over-provisioning from predefined types.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Compute Engine custom machine types let you specify the exact number of vCPUs and amount of memory your workload needs. This eliminates the cost waste of over-provisioning with a larger predefined type. Option A is incorrect because custom configurations are fully supported. Option C adds unnecessary complexity with load balancing across two VMs. Option D wastes money paying for unused resources. Memory must fall between 0.9 GB and 6.5 GB per vCPU in the standard range, with extended memory available for higher ratios at additional cost.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Custom machine types are available in N1, N2, N2D, and E2 machine families; the vCPU count must be 1 or an even number, and memory must be in multiples of 256 MB.
  • Extended memory configurations allow up to 8 GB per vCPU (beyond the standard 6.5 GB limit) at an additional per-GB premium, useful for workloads like in-memory caching that need more RAM than the standard ratio permits.
  • Custom machine types are priced per vCPU and per GB of memory independently, so you pay only for what you configure rather than a bundled predefined price, often resulting in 5-20% savings over the nearest predefined type.
  • Use the GCP Pricing Calculator or the gcloud compute machine-types describe command to compare custom type costs against predefined alternatives before committing to a configuration.

questions.title: Preemptible VMs
questions.scenario: A batch processing job can tolerate interruptions and needs to minimize costs. The job can checkpoint and resume if interrupted.
questions.questionText: Which VM type offers the lowest cost for fault-tolerant batch workloads?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Look for the VM type that uses excess Compute Engine capacity at steep discounts of 60-91%, accepting the trade-off that Google can reclaim the instance at any time.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Spot VMs (the evolution of legacy preemptible VMs) leverage excess Compute Engine capacity at 60-91% discounts compared to on-demand pricing. They can be preempted with a 30-second warning when Google needs the capacity back. Standard on-demand VMs (B) cost full price. Sole-tenant nodes (C) are premium-priced dedicated hardware for compliance needs. Committed use VMs (D) offer 57-70% discounts but require 1-3 year commitments and are designed for steady-state workloads, not interruptible batch jobs. Since the scenario explicitly states fault tolerance with checkpointing, Spot VMs provide the lowest cost.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Spot VMs have no minimum or maximum runtime, unlike legacy preemptible VMs which had a hard 24-hour limit; they persist until preempted or manually stopped, making them more flexible for variable-length batch jobs.
  • Best practice is to use shutdown scripts (configured via metadata) to checkpoint application state to Cloud Storage or Persistent Disk before the VM is terminated, enabling seamless job resumption on a new instance.
  • Combine Spot VMs with managed instance groups (MIGs) that automatically recreate preempted instances, and use Cloud Pub/Sub or Cloud Tasks to manage the work queue for distributed batch processing.
  • Spot VM pricing varies by machine type and zone; use the Bulk Instance API or instance templates with Spot provisioning model to efficiently launch large fleets of interruptible workers.

questions.title: Committed Use Discounts
questions.scenario: Your company runs steady-state production workloads that require consistent compute capacity for the next three years.
questions.questionText: Which pricing model provides the best discount for predictable long-term workloads?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: For workloads with predictable, steady-state resource needs over multiple years, the deepest discounts come from committing to a minimum usage level for a defined contract term.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Committed use discounts (CUDs) provide up to 57% off for 1-year commitments and up to 70% off for 3-year commitments on Compute Engine resources. On-demand pricing (A) has no discount. Sustained use discounts (B) are automatic but cap at 30% and require no commitment, making them weaker for truly steady workloads. Spot VM pricing (C) offers steep discounts but instances can be preempted at any time, which is unacceptable for production. Since the scenario describes a three-year steady-state production workload, the 3-year CUD delivers the deepest guaranteed savings.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CUDs come in two forms: resource-based (commit to specific vCPU and memory amounts) and spend-based (commit to a minimum dollar spend), with spend-based CUDs offering more flexibility across machine families and regions.
  • Resource-based CUDs are regional and apply automatically across all projects within that region that share the same billing account, so you do not need to assign them to specific VMs.
  • Sustained use discounts (SUDs) and CUDs do not stack; GCP applies whichever discount is greater, so CUD-covered usage does not also receive SUD benefits.
  • CUDs cannot be canceled once purchased, so accurate capacity forecasting is critical; over-commitment means paying for unused resources, while under-commitment leaves savings on the table.

questions.title: App Engine Standard Environment
questions.scenario: A startup wants to deploy a Python web application without managing servers. They expect variable traffic and want to pay only when the app is handling requests.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service automatically scales to zero and charges only for actual usage?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Focus on which App Engine environment can scale all the way down to zero running instances when there is no traffic, ensuring you are not billed during idle periods.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: App Engine standard environment is a fully managed PaaS that automatically scales instances up and down based on traffic, including scaling to zero when idle so you pay nothing during quiet periods. Compute Engine with autoscaling (B) always has at least one VM running. App Engine flexible environment (C) runs on Compute Engine VMs and requires a minimum of one instance, so it never scales to zero. GKE Autopilot (D) charges per pod resources and involves Kubernetes operational complexity. For a startup wanting zero-management, pay-per-request pricing with Python support, App Engine standard is the ideal fit.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• App Engine standard uses sandboxed runtimes with fast startup times (milliseconds to seconds), enabling rapid scale-out during traffic spikes and quick scale-to-zero during lulls.
  • Supported languages include Python 3, Java 11/17, Node.js, PHP, Ruby, and Go; each runtime has specific constraints on library usage and system call access due to the sandboxed execution model.
  • App Engine flexible environment runs custom Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs with startup times measured in minutes, charges for the underlying VM regardless of request volume, and does not scale to zero.
  • App Engine standard provides automatic versioning with traffic splitting (by IP, cookie, or random), letting you canary-test new versions before full rollout without managing infrastructure.

questions.title: App Engine Flexible vs Standard
questions.scenario: A team needs to deploy a web application that uses custom C++ libraries and requires WebSocket support.
questions.questionText: Which App Engine environment supports custom runtimes and native WebSocket connections?

choices.text: Both environments support custom runtimes equally

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: One App Engine environment runs your code in Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs, giving you the freedom to use any language, library, or binary including native WebSocket connections.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: App Engine flexible environment runs your application in Docker containers on managed Compute Engine VMs, allowing custom runtimes with any language or native library including C++ and WebSocket support. Standard environment (B) uses sandboxed runtimes that restrict available libraries and do not natively support WebSockets. Option C is wrong because flexible environment handles this scenario without requiring raw Compute Engine management. Option D is incorrect because standard has significantly more runtime restrictions than flexible. The trade-off is that flexible has slower scaling (minutes vs seconds) and higher minimum cost since it always runs at least one instance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Flexible environment instances take 1-5 minutes to start because they spin up full Compute Engine VMs with Docker, while standard environment instances start in milliseconds to seconds using lightweight sandboxed containers.
  • Flexible environment pricing is based on the underlying Compute Engine VM resources (vCPU, memory, disk), while standard environment uses instance-hours pricing with automatic scaling that can reach zero cost during idle periods.
  • Flexible supports SSH access to running instances for debugging, custom health checks, and the ability to write to the local filesystem temporarily, none of which are available in standard.
  • Standard environment recently added WebSocket support for some runtimes (Python 3, Java 11+, Node.js), but flexible remains the better choice when you need arbitrary native binaries, system packages, or unrestricted filesystem access.

questions.title: Cloud Functions Use Case
questions.scenario: A developer needs to automatically resize images uploaded to Cloud Storage without maintaining any servers.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service is best suited for running event-triggered code without managing infrastructure?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Look for the fully serverless, Functions-as-a-Service (FaaS) offering that executes small units of code automatically in response to events from other GCP services like Cloud Storage.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Functions is GCP's serverless, event-driven compute service designed for exactly this pattern: trigger code execution in response to Cloud Storage events like file uploads. You deploy just the function code with no servers, containers, or clusters to manage. Cloud Composer (A) is a managed Apache Airflow service for orchestrating complex workflows, not individual event handlers. Compute Engine (B) requires provisioning and managing VMs. GKE (D) requires managing Kubernetes clusters. For a simple event-triggered task like image resizing, Cloud Functions delivers the lowest operational overhead and pay-per-invocation pricing.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Functions 2nd gen is built on Cloud Run under the hood, providing longer timeouts (up to 60 minutes vs 9 minutes for 1st gen), larger memory (up to 32 GB), and support for concurrent request handling per instance.
  • Supported runtimes include Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, and PHP; the function receives the event payload (e.g., the Cloud Storage object metadata) as input parameters automatically.
  • Functions scale automatically from zero to thousands of instances based on incoming events, and you pay only for compute time during execution (billed per 100ms) plus a small per-invocation charge.
  • For the image-resize pattern specifically, the function is triggered by a finalize event on the source bucket, processes the image using a library like Pillow or Sharp, and writes the resized output to a destination bucket to avoid infinite trigger loops.

questions.title: Cloud Functions Triggers
questions.scenario: You need to process messages from a Pub/Sub topic and also expose an HTTP endpoint for external API calls.
questions.questionText: How can Cloud Functions be triggered?

choices.text: Both HTTP requests and event triggers (Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, etc.)

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Functions supports two broad categories of triggers: direct HTTP invocation via a URL endpoint and event-based triggers from GCP services like Pub/Sub and Cloud Storage.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Functions can be triggered by HTTP requests (providing a unique URL endpoint for direct invocation) or by events from GCP services like Cloud Storage uploads, Pub/Sub messages, Firestore changes, and Firebase events. Option A is wrong because event triggers are a core capability. Option C is wrong because HTTP triggers are equally fundamental. Option D is incorrect because Cloud Scheduler is just one way to invoke HTTP functions on a schedule, not the only trigger mechanism. The scenario requires both patterns: a Pub/Sub event trigger for message processing and an HTTP trigger for the external API endpoint.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• HTTP functions receive a unique URL endpoint (https://REGION-PROJECT.cloudfunctions.net/FUNCTION_NAME) and can be secured with IAM authentication or left publicly accessible; event functions subscribe to event sources via push delivery.
  • Cloud Functions 2nd gen uses Eventarc as its event routing layer, supporting 90+ event sources including Cloud Audit Logs, enabling triggers on virtually any GCP API action (e.g., a BigQuery job completing or a VM being created).
  • Use Cloud Scheduler with HTTP functions to create cron-like scheduled executions; Cloud Scheduler sends an HTTP POST to the function URL on your defined schedule, combining time-based and event-based patterns.
  • For Pub/Sub triggers, the function receives the message payload as a base64-encoded data field with attributes; the function must acknowledge processing by returning successfully, or the message is retried according to the subscription's retry policy.

questions.title: Cloud Run Overview
questions.scenario: A team wants to deploy containerized applications without managing Kubernetes clusters, with automatic scaling and pay-per-use pricing.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service runs containers in a fully managed serverless environment?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Identify the GCP service that provides a fully managed serverless platform where you deploy any container image and it scales automatically, including down to zero, without any cluster management.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Run is GCP's fully managed serverless container platform. You deploy any container image and Cloud Run handles scaling (including to zero), load balancing, TLS termination, and infrastructure management. GKE Standard (A) requires managing Kubernetes clusters and node pools. App Engine standard (B) uses managed runtimes, not arbitrary containers. Compute Engine with containers (C) still requires VM provisioning and management. Cloud Run uniquely combines the flexibility of containers (any language, any library) with the operational simplicity of serverless, charging only for resources consumed during request processing.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Run is built on Knative, the open-source Kubernetes-based serverless platform, providing portability to any Knative-compatible environment including on-premises GKE clusters via Cloud Run for Anthos.
  • Supports any language or library that can be packaged in a container conforming to the Cloud Run container contract: listen on the PORT environment variable, handle HTTP requests, and be stateless between requests.
  • Cloud Run services handle HTTP/gRPC traffic with automatic TLS, custom domains, and revision-based traffic splitting for canary deployments; Cloud Run jobs handle batch workloads that run to completion without serving requests.
  • Pricing is based on vCPU-seconds, memory GiB-seconds, and request count, with a generous free tier (2 million requests/month); idle minimum instances are billed at a reduced rate compared to actively serving instances.

questions.title: Cloud Run vs Cloud Functions
questions.scenario: You need to run a containerized application that handles HTTP requests and requires custom system libraries. The application has complex dependencies.
questions.questionText: Why might Cloud Run be preferred over Cloud Functions for this scenario?

choices.text: Cloud Functions cannot handle HTTP requests
Cloud Functions has better scaling capabilities
Cloud Run supports any container image with any dependencies
Cloud Run is always cheaper than Cloud Functions

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Run accepts any container image you build, giving you unrestricted control over the runtime, system libraries, and dependencies, whereas Cloud Functions limits you to specific supported runtimes.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Run accepts any container image, giving you full control over the runtime environment, system-level dependencies, and installed libraries. Cloud Functions constrains you to specific supported runtimes and may not support all native system libraries your application needs. Option B is wrong because both services autoscale effectively. Option C is incorrect because pricing depends on usage patterns; Functions can be cheaper for lightweight event processing. Option D is false because Cloud Functions fully supports HTTP triggers. For applications with complex or unusual dependencies, Cloud Run's container flexibility is the decisive advantage.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Functions 2nd gen is actually built on Cloud Run under the hood, meaning the underlying infrastructure is the same; the difference is in the developer experience and the constraints each surface imposes.
  • Cloud Run supports request timeouts up to 60 minutes and allows multiple concurrent requests per container instance (up to 1000), while Cloud Functions 1st gen is limited to 9-minute timeouts and processes one request at a time per instance.
  • Cloud Run allows you to configure CPU allocation to be always-on (charged continuously) for background processing, or request-based (charged only during request handling), giving you more control over cost and compute behavior.
  • Choose Cloud Functions when you want the simplest developer experience for lightweight event-driven logic; choose Cloud Run when you need container-level control, longer execution times, gRPC support, or WebSocket connections.

questions.title: GKE Overview
questions.scenario: A company wants to run containerized microservices with full Kubernetes features including custom resource definitions and service mesh.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides managed Kubernetes clusters?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Look for GCP's managed Kubernetes service that handles the control plane, automatic upgrades, and deep integration with GCP while giving you full access to the Kubernetes API.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) provides fully managed Kubernetes clusters where Google handles the control plane, etcd storage, upgrades, and security patches. You get full Kubernetes API access including CRDs, operators, and service meshes like Istio/Anthos Service Mesh. Compute Engine (A) provides raw VMs without orchestration. Cloud Run (B) is serverless and hides Kubernetes complexity. App Engine flexible (C) runs containers but does not expose Kubernetes features. When the scenario requires full Kubernetes capabilities like CRDs and service mesh, GKE is the only appropriate choice.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GKE offers two modes: Standard (you manage node pools, machine types, and scaling policies) and Autopilot (Google manages all node infrastructure and you pay per pod resource request, with built-in security hardening).
  • GKE integrates deeply with GCP services: Cloud Build for CI/CD, Artifact Registry for container images, Binary Authorization for deploy-time image attestation, and Cloud Logging/Monitoring for observability.
  • The GKE control plane is managed by Google at no charge for Autopilot and at a fixed hourly rate for Standard mode, with an SLA of 99.95% for regional clusters and 99.5% for zonal clusters.
  • GKE supports multi-cluster management via GKE Hub (Connect/Fleet), enabling consistent policy enforcement, configuration sync, and service mesh across multiple clusters and even hybrid/multi-cloud environments.

questions.title: GKE Autopilot vs Standard
questions.scenario: A team wants to run Kubernetes workloads with minimal operational overhead. They prefer paying only for the pods they run, not for node capacity.
questions.questionText: Which GKE mode should they use?

choices.text: GKE Standard with manual node management

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: One GKE mode fully manages the node infrastructure for you, charges per pod resource request rather than per node, and enforces security best practices by default.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GKE Autopilot is a mode where Google manages the entire cluster infrastructure including node provisioning, scaling, and security hardening. You pay only for the CPU, memory, and ephemeral storage that your pods request, not for idle node capacity. Cloud Run (A) is serverless but does not provide full Kubernetes features. GKE Standard with manual management (B) requires you to size and manage nodes. GKE Standard with cluster autoscaler (C) still charges for node-level resources and requires node pool configuration decisions. Autopilot eliminates node-level operations entirely while retaining full Kubernetes API compatibility.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Autopilot enforces security best practices by default: no SSH access to nodes, no privileged containers, no host namespace sharing, mandatory resource requests on all pods, and automatic security patching of the node OS.
  • Autopilot pricing is per vCPU-hour and per GiB-hour consumed by pod resource requests; if a pod requests 1 vCPU and 2 GiB memory, you pay for exactly that even if the underlying node has unused capacity.
  • Standard mode gives more control (custom node images, GPU node pools, SSH access, DaemonSets without restrictions), making it better for workloads needing privileged access or specialized hardware configurations.
  • Autopilot supports Spot Pods for cost savings on fault-tolerant workloads, applying the same preemption model as Spot VMs but at the pod scheduling level within the managed node infrastructure.

questions.title: GKE Node Pools
questions.scenario: You need to run ML training jobs requiring GPUs alongside web services that need standard CPUs in the same GKE cluster.
questions.questionText: How should you configure the GKE cluster to support both workload types?

choices.text: GKE does not support mixed machine types
Use a single node pool with the largest machine type
Create separate node pools with different machine types and use node selectors
Create separate clusters for each workload type

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GKE clusters can contain multiple node pools, each with different machine types and hardware configurations, allowing you to run diverse workloads by directing pods to the right pool.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GKE node pools are groups of nodes within a cluster that share the same configuration. You can create multiple node pools with different machine types: a standard CPU pool for web services and a GPU-enabled pool (e.g., A2 or G2 machine types) for ML training. Kubernetes node selectors or node affinity rules then direct pods to the appropriate pool. Using a single large node pool (B) wastes GPU resources on web workloads. Separate clusters (C) adds unnecessary management overhead and network complexity. Option D is factually incorrect. Multiple node pools within a single cluster is the standard and recommended pattern.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use Kubernetes taints and tolerations alongside node selectors to prevent non-GPU workloads from being scheduled on expensive GPU nodes: taint the GPU pool with nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule and add matching tolerations only to ML training pods.
  • Each node pool can have its own independent autoscaling configuration (min/max nodes), allowing the GPU pool to scale to zero when no training jobs are running, eliminating idle GPU costs.
  • Node auto-provisioning (NAP) can automatically create new node pools with the right machine types based on pending pod resource requests, removing the need to pre-create pools for every possible configuration.
  • For GPU workloads, install the NVIDIA GPU device plugin DaemonSet (auto-installed on GKE) and specify nvidia.com/gpu in pod resource requests to ensure proper GPU scheduling and isolation between training jobs.

questions.title: Managed Instance Groups
questions.scenario: You need to deploy a stateless web application across multiple VMs with automatic healing and load distribution.
questions.questionText: Which Compute Engine feature manages groups of identical VM instances?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The feature you need creates and manages a fleet of identical VM instances from a single template, providing built-in autoscaling, autohealing, and rolling update capabilities.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) create and manage groups of identical VM instances based on an instance template. MIGs provide autoscaling (adjusting instance count based on metrics), autohealing (replacing unhealthy instances detected by health checks), and rolling updates for zero-downtime deployments. Unmanaged instance groups (A) contain heterogeneous VMs you manage manually without autoscaling. VM Templates (B) is not a standalone feature; instance templates define configuration but do not manage instances. Sole-tenant nodes (C) provide dedicated hardware but are not an instance management mechanism.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• MIGs come in two varieties: zonal (instances in a single zone) and regional (instances automatically distributed across up to 3 zones in a region for high availability and zone-failure resilience).
  • Autohealing uses configurable health checks (HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP) with customizable check intervals, thresholds, and initial delays; when a VM fails health checks, the MIG automatically deletes and recreates it from the instance template.
  • Unmanaged instance groups are used only for pre-existing heterogeneous VMs that you need to place behind a load balancer; they lack autoscaling, autohealing, and rolling update features entirely.
  • MIGs integrate with Cloud Load Balancing as backend services, enabling automatic registration/deregistration of instances as the group scales, with connection draining during scale-in to avoid dropping active requests.

questions.title: MIG Autoscaling Policies
questions.scenario: Your web application needs to scale based on the number of requests per second, maintaining an average of 100 RPS per instance.
questions.questionText: Which autoscaling metric should you configure for the managed instance group?

choices.text: HTTP load balancing serving capacity with target utilization

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When you need to scale based on requests per second per instance, use the load balancing serving capacity metric which directly maps incoming request rates to instance count targets.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: MIG autoscaling supports multiple metrics including CPU utilization, memory utilization, load balancing serving capacity, Pub/Sub queue depth, and custom Cloud Monitoring metrics. For scaling based on HTTP requests per second, use the load balancing serving capacity metric with a target RPS per instance. CPU utilization only (A) does not directly correlate to request count and may scale incorrectly for I/O-bound applications. Memory utilization only (C) is irrelevant to request rate. A fixed instance count (D) does not scale at all. The load balancing metric is purpose-built for request-rate-driven scaling.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• When multiple scaling metrics are configured simultaneously, the MIG autoscaler calculates the required instance count for each metric independently and uses the highest value, ensuring no metric is under-served.
  • Scale-in controls let you set a maximum rate at which instances are removed (e.g., no more than 10% per 10 minutes), preventing rapid scale-down during temporary traffic dips that could cause capacity problems when traffic returns.
  • Predictive autoscaling uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively scale out before anticipated demand spikes, reducing cold-start latency for traffic that follows predictable daily or weekly cycles.
  • Custom Cloud Monitoring metrics (e.g., application-specific queue depth, processing latency) can drive autoscaling via the Stackdriver Monitoring API, enabling scaling behavior tailored to business-specific performance indicators.

questions.title: Regional MIGs
questions.scenario: You need to deploy a stateless application that remains available even if an entire zone fails.
questions.questionText: Which configuration provides zone-level fault tolerance for managed instance groups?

choices.text: Regional managed instance group spread across multiple zones
Zonal managed instance group with larger instances
Multiple separate zonal MIGs with manual failover
Single VM with high availability enabled

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: A regional MIG automatically distributes instances across multiple zones within a region, so if one zone experiences an outage, instances in the remaining zones continue serving traffic.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Regional managed instance groups automatically distribute VM instances across multiple zones in a region (up to 3 zones). If a zone fails, instances in healthy zones continue serving traffic and the autoscaler creates replacement instances in those zones to maintain target capacity. A zonal MIG with larger instances (A) provides no zone-level redundancy. Multiple separate zonal MIGs with manual failover (C) requires custom orchestration and is error-prone. A single VM (D) is a single point of failure regardless of its configuration. Regional MIGs are the built-in, fully automated solution for zone-level fault tolerance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Regional MIGs distribute instances evenly across zones by default (EVEN distribution); use the target distribution shape setting to configure BALANCED (proportional to zone capacity) or ANY (fill cheapest zones first) for cost-optimized or capacity-aware distribution.
  • Combine regional MIGs with regional external or internal HTTP(S) load balancers for automatic, seamless failover; the load balancer health checks detect unhealthy instances and route traffic only to healthy ones across all zones.
  • During a zone outage, the regional MIG autoscaler compensates by creating additional instances in the remaining healthy zones to maintain the configured target size, ensuring overall capacity is preserved.
  • Regional MIGs require regional instance templates (or global templates with regional disks) to avoid cross-zone resource dependencies that could cause creation failures when a zone is down.

questions.title: GKE Cluster Autoscaler
questions.scenario: Your GKE cluster has pods pending due to insufficient resources, but the current nodes are fully utilized.
questions.questionText: What does the GKE cluster autoscaler do in this situation?

choices.text: Increases CPU limits on existing nodes
Adds new nodes to accommodate pending pods

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The cluster autoscaler monitors for pods in a Pending state due to insufficient node resources and responds by adding new nodes to the node pool to accommodate the unschedulable pods.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The GKE cluster autoscaler detects pods that cannot be scheduled because existing nodes lack sufficient CPU, memory, or GPU resources, and automatically adds new nodes to the appropriate node pool. It also removes underutilized nodes when their pods can be rescheduled elsewhere, reducing costs. Option B is wrong because you cannot increase CPU limits on existing nodes, which are fixed by machine type. Option C is incorrect because the cluster autoscaler operates within a single cluster. Option D describes Kubernetes pod preemption (priority-based eviction), which is a separate mechanism from cluster autoscaling.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Configure min and max node counts per node pool to control scaling bounds; the autoscaler will not exceed the max even if pods remain pending, and will not drop below the min even if nodes are underutilized.
  • Pod disruption budgets (PDBs) control how aggressively the autoscaler can remove underutilized nodes during scale-down; PDBs specify the minimum number of pods that must remain available, preventing the autoscaler from evicting critical workloads.
  • Node auto-provisioning (NAP) goes a step further than cluster autoscaling by automatically creating entirely new node pools with appropriate machine types, GPU configurations, or Spot provisioning based on the resource requirements of pending pods.
  • The autoscaler evaluates scale-down candidates based on utilization thresholds (default 50%) and a stabilization window (default 10 minutes) to avoid thrashing; nodes with system-critical pods, local storage, or pods without controllers are not removed.

questions.title: Instance Templates
questions.scenario: You need to ensure all VMs in your managed instance group have identical configurations including machine type, disk, and startup script.
questions.questionText: What should you create to define the VM configuration for a managed instance group?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The resource that defines VM properties like machine type, boot disk, networking, and metadata for use by managed instance groups is immutable once created and must be versioned for updates.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Instance templates are immutable resources that define all VM properties including machine type, boot disk image, network configuration, service account, labels, and metadata (such as startup scripts). MIGs use instance templates to create identical instances. A machine image (A) captures the full VM state including multiple disks but is used for backup/cloning, not MIG configuration. A custom image (B) captures only the boot disk contents. A snapshot (C) is a point-in-time copy of a single disk. Only instance templates provide the complete VM specification that MIGs require for consistent instance creation.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Instance templates are immutable: you cannot edit an existing template. To change VM configuration, create a new instance template version and update the MIG to use it via a rolling update, canary update, or opportunistic update policy.
  • Use regional instance templates for regional MIGs to avoid cross-zone resource dependencies; global templates work but may reference resources (like disks) that are zone-specific, causing failures in some zones.
  • Machine images capture everything about a VM (boot disk, additional disks, configuration, permissions, metadata) and are useful for disaster recovery or cloning, but they are too heavyweight and mutable for the repeatable instance creation that MIGs need.
  • Instance templates support metadata variables and startup-script-url references to Cloud Storage, enabling parameterized configurations where the same template can bootstrap different application roles based on instance metadata.

questions.title: GPU Workloads
questions.scenario: A machine learning team needs to train deep learning models and requires NVIDIA GPUs attached to their VMs.
questions.questionText: How do you add GPUs to Compute Engine VMs?

choices.text: GPUs can only be used with Kubernetes, not raw VMs
GPUs are automatically available on all machine types
Attach GPUs to supported machine types and install GPU drivers
Use special GPU-only VMs that cannot have CPUs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GPUs are added to specific supported Compute Engine machine types during VM creation, and you must install the appropriate NVIDIA drivers (or use a pre-configured deep learning VM image) before the GPU is usable.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GPUs can be attached to supported Compute Engine machine types when creating or configuring a VM. You select the GPU type and count, and the GPU becomes available once NVIDIA drivers are installed. Option A is wrong because Compute Engine fully supports GPUs on raw VMs, not just in Kubernetes. Option B is incorrect because GPUs are available only on specific machine families and require explicit attachment. Option C is false because GPU-equipped VMs always include CPUs. GPU availability varies by zone, so check zone-level availability before creating GPU instances. Deep Learning VM images come with pre-installed drivers and ML frameworks for quick setup.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Accelerator-optimized A2 machine types have NVIDIA A100 GPUs built in (up to 16 per VM), and G2 machine types have NVIDIA L4 GPUs built in; these machine families do not allow adding or removing GPUs since the GPU configuration is fixed per machine type.
  • N1 machine types support attaching NVIDIA T4, P4, P100, V100, and K80 GPUs as accelerators, with the GPU count configurable at VM creation time; other machine families (E2, N2, C3) do not support GPU attachment.
  • Use Deep Learning VM images (available in the Cloud Console image gallery) for pre-installed NVIDIA drivers, CUDA toolkit, cuDNN, and popular ML frameworks like TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX, eliminating driver compatibility issues.
  • GPU-attached VMs cannot be live migrated during host maintenance events; set the on-host-maintenance policy to TERMINATE with automatic-restart enabled so the VM restarts on a healthy host after maintenance completes.

questions.title: TPU for ML Training
questions.scenario: Your team is training large transformer models and needs to accelerate training beyond what GPUs can provide cost-effectively.
questions.questionText: Which Google Cloud hardware accelerator is specifically designed for machine learning workloads at scale?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Google designed custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) specifically for accelerating machine learning training and inference, offering superior performance per dollar for large-scale model workloads.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) are Google's custom-developed ASICs designed specifically for accelerating machine learning workloads. They excel at large-scale training and inference for models built with TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch. High-memory VMs (A) provide RAM but no ML acceleration. FPGAs (B) are not offered as a standard GCP compute accelerator. Standard CPUs with AVX-512 (C) provide some SIMD acceleration but are orders of magnitude slower than TPUs for matrix operations. TPU pods can scale to thousands of interconnected chips for distributed training of the largest foundation models.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• TPU generations include v2 (45 TFLOPS), v3 (123 TFLOPS), v4 (275 TFLOPS bfloat16), and v5e (optimized for cost-efficient inference); each generation improves both raw performance and memory bandwidth for larger model sizes.
  • Cloud TPU VMs provide direct SSH access to the host machine connected to the TPU, eliminating the network overhead of the older TPU Node architecture where a separate Compute Engine VM communicated with the TPU over gRPC.
  • TPU pods interconnect hundreds or thousands of TPU chips via high-bandwidth custom interconnects (ICI), enabling data-parallel and model-parallel distributed training of models with billions or trillions of parameters.
  • TPUs are most cost-effective for workloads that can leverage bfloat16 (brain floating point) precision and large batch sizes; workloads requiring high-precision float32 arithmetic or small batch sizes may perform better on NVIDIA GPUs.

questions.title: Sustained Use Discounts
questions.scenario: Your VMs run continuously throughout the month. You want automatic discounts without making commitments.
questions.questionText: Which discount is automatically applied to VMs running for a significant portion of the month?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP automatically applies incremental discounts to VMs that run for more than 25% of a billing month, with no commitment or upfront action required from you.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Sustained use discounts (SUDs) are automatic discounts applied to Compute Engine VMs and GKE nodes that run for more than 25% of a billing month. The discount increases with usage, reaching up to 30% for instances running the entire month. Committed use discounts (B) require a 1 or 3-year commitment and are not automatic. Spot VM pricing (C) requires opting into preemptible instances. Free tier credits (D) are limited introductory credits, not a discount mechanism. SUDs require zero configuration; GCP calculates and applies them automatically to your bill based on observed usage.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SUDs are calculated separately for vCPUs and memory, and are aggregated across all instances of the same machine type family within a region, so stopping one N2 VM and starting another still accumulates toward the same SUD threshold.
  • E2 and A2 machine types do not receive sustained use discounts; E2 has built-in lower pricing, and A2 (GPU-optimized) uses separate pricing. Check which machine families are eligible before relying on SUDs for cost planning.
  • SUDs and CUDs do not stack: GCP applies whichever discount is greater for a given resource-hour. If you have a CUD covering your base usage, SUDs only apply to on-demand usage that exceeds the CUD commitment.
  • SUDs are applied per billing account and aggregated across all projects in a region, meaning fragmented workloads across multiple projects still benefit from combined usage toward the discount tiers.

questions.title: Right-sizing Recommendations
questions.scenario: Your VMs have been running for several weeks, and you suspect many are over-provisioned based on actual usage patterns.
questions.questionText: Which GCP tool provides recommendations for optimizing VM sizes based on actual usage?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP has a built-in recommendation engine that analyzes VM utilization metrics over time and suggests optimal machine type changes to reduce costs without impacting performance.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GCP Recommender analyzes VM CPU, memory, and disk utilization metrics over time (typically 8 days minimum of data) and provides right-sizing recommendations to reduce costs. It suggests smaller machine types for consistently underutilized VMs and identifies idle VMs that can be stopped or deleted. Cloud Profiler (A) analyzes application code performance, not infrastructure sizing. Cloud Trace (C) tracks request latency across distributed services. Cloud Debugger (D) inspects application state at runtime. Only the Recommender service is designed to analyze infrastructure utilization patterns and suggest cost-optimal VM configurations.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Recommendations appear in the Cloud Console VM instances page, via the gcloud recommender recommendations list command, and through the Recommender API, enabling programmatic integration with infrastructure-as-code pipelines for automated right-sizing.
  • Recommender provides multiple recommendation types beyond VM right-sizing: idle resource cleanup (unused disks, static IPs, load balancers), committed use discount purchase suggestions, and IAM policy tightening recommendations.
  • Each recommendation includes an estimated monthly cost savings, a confidence level (based on data quality and observation period), and the specific machine type change suggested, making it easy to prioritize high-impact changes.
  • If recommendations suggest non-standard vCPU/memory ratios, consider custom machine types to precisely match the recommended configuration rather than jumping to the next predefined machine type, which may still over-provision.

questions.title: Cloud Run Concurrency
questions.scenario: Your Cloud Run service handles requests that are CPU-intensive. You want to ensure each container instance handles only one request at a time.
questions.questionText: Which Cloud Run setting controls how many concurrent requests a single container instance handles?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Run has a per-instance concurrency setting that controls how many simultaneous requests a single container instance can process, directly affecting scaling behavior and resource utilization.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The Cloud Run container instance concurrency setting (configurable from 1 to 1000) determines how many requests a single container instance handles simultaneously. For CPU-intensive work, setting concurrency to 1 ensures each instance processes one request at a time, preventing resource contention. Maximum instances (A) caps total instances, not per-instance concurrency. Minimum instances (B) controls cold start mitigation. CPU allocation (C) determines when CPU is available (request-time only vs always), not request routing. Setting concurrency to 1 means Cloud Run creates a new instance for each concurrent request, trading higher instance count for predictable per-request performance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The default concurrency is 80; higher concurrency means fewer total instances are needed to handle the same traffic, reducing cold starts and lowering per-request cost since instance overhead is amortized across more requests.
  • For I/O-bound workloads (database queries, API calls, file reads), high concurrency (80-250) is optimal because the CPU is idle while waiting for I/O; for CPU-bound workloads (image processing, computation), concurrency of 1-4 prevents thread starvation.
  • Your application code must be thread-safe to use concurrency greater than 1; if the application uses global mutable state or non-thread-safe libraries, set concurrency to 1 to avoid race conditions and data corruption.
  • Cloud Run autoscaler uses the formula: target instances = concurrent requests / concurrency setting. With 100 concurrent requests and concurrency of 1, Cloud Run targets 100 instances; with concurrency of 50, it targets only 2 instances.

questions.title: Cloud Run Minimum Instances
questions.scenario: Your Cloud Run service experiences latency spikes when scaling from zero after periods of no traffic.
questions.questionText: How can you reduce cold start latency for your Cloud Run service?

choices.text: Set minimum instances to keep containers warm
Cold starts cannot be mitigated in Cloud Run

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Setting a minimum instance count greater than zero keeps container instances warm and ready to handle requests immediately, eliminating the cold start delay when traffic arrives after an idle period.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Setting minimum instances greater than 0 keeps container instances running and warm, ready to handle requests instantly without cold start overhead. Reducing image size (A) helps reduce cold start duration but does not eliminate it when scaling from zero. Increasing maximum instances (C) controls the upper scaling bound, not cold start behavior. Option D is factually wrong since multiple mitigation strategies exist. The trade-off is cost: idle minimum instances incur charges at a reduced rate. The optimal minimum instance count balances your latency SLA requirements against the additional cost of keeping instances warm.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Idle minimum instances are billed at a reduced rate (CPU is not charged when idle in request-based CPU allocation mode, but memory is still billed), making the cost significantly lower than actively serving instances.
  • Enable startup CPU boost to temporarily allocate additional CPU during container initialization, speeding up framework loading, JIT compilation, and dependency initialization that make cold starts slow for heavy applications.
  • Optimize container images for faster cold starts: use distroless or Alpine base images, implement lazy loading for large dependencies, minimize initialization work in the application startup path, and precompile any bytecode offline.
  • Cloud Run also supports execution environment selection: gen1 (gVisor sandbox, faster cold starts for small containers) and gen2 (full Linux kernel, better for workloads needing system calls or large memory), which affects cold start characteristics.

questions.title: Persistent Disks
questions.scenario: A VM needs storage that persists independently of the VM lifecycle and can be resized without downtime.
questions.questionText: Which storage option provides durable block storage for Compute Engine VMs?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The block storage option that persists independently of the VM, survives VM deletion, supports online resizing, and provides automatic encryption and snapshot capabilities is network-attached rather than physically attached.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Persistent Disks are durable, network-attached block storage devices for Compute Engine VMs. They persist independently of VMs, meaning data survives VM deletion. They support online resizing (increasing size without downtime), snapshots for backup, and can be attached to multiple VMs in read-only mode or moved between VMs. Local SSDs (B) provide high IOPS but data is lost when the VM stops. Cloud Storage buckets (C) are object storage, not block storage, and cannot be mounted as a filesystem natively. RAM disks (D) lose data when the VM stops and are limited by available memory.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Persistent Disk types include pd-standard (HDD, lowest cost, sequential workloads), pd-balanced (SSD, good price-performance), pd-ssd (SSD, high IOPS), and pd-extreme (highest configurable IOPS up to 120K, for databases like SAP HANA and Oracle).
  • Regional persistent disks replicate data synchronously across two zones within a region, providing high availability for stateful workloads and enabling automatic failover without data loss when used with regional MIGs.
  • Persistent Disk performance (IOPS and throughput) scales with disk size: larger disks provide higher performance up to per-VM limits, so under-provisioning disk size can bottleneck application I/O even if capacity is sufficient.
  • Snapshots are incremental (only changed blocks are stored after the first full snapshot), support cross-region replication for disaster recovery, and can be scheduled automatically using snapshot schedules attached to the disk resource.

questions.title: Local SSDs vs Persistent Disks
questions.scenario: A database workload requires extremely low latency storage and high IOPS. Data is replicated at the application level, so disk-level durability is not required.
questions.questionText: Which storage type provides the lowest latency for Compute Engine VMs?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The lowest-latency storage option for Compute Engine is physically attached to the host server, delivering sub-millisecond access times and millions of IOPS, but the data is ephemeral and lost when the VM stops.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Local SSDs are NVMe or SCSI drives physically attached to the server hosting your VM, providing the lowest possible latency and highest IOPS available on Compute Engine. However, data on local SSDs is ephemeral: it is lost when the VM stops, is preempted, or the host fails. SSD Persistent Disk (A) offers good performance but higher latency than local SSD due to network attachment. Standard Persistent Disk (B) is HDD-backed with the highest latency. Extreme Persistent Disk (C) offers high configurable IOPS but still has network latency. Since the scenario states data is replicated at the application level, the ephemeral nature of local SSDs is acceptable.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Local SSDs provide up to 9 TB per VM (24 x 375 GB drives) with up to 2.4 million read IOPS and 1.2 million write IOPS, far exceeding any Persistent Disk type's capabilities for latency-sensitive workloads.
  • Local SSDs are included as built-in storage on Z3 machine types (optimized for storage-intensive workloads like databases) and can be attached to N1, N2, N2D, C2, C2D, and M3 machine types at creation time only.
  • Data on local SSDs is encrypted at rest automatically by Google, but the drives cannot be detached, moved to another VM, or snapshotted; if you need to preserve data, you must copy it to Persistent Disk or Cloud Storage before stopping the VM.
  • Common use cases include high-performance caches (Redis, Memcached), scratch space for data processing, and databases with built-in replication (Cassandra, CockroachDB, Elasticsearch) where application-level redundancy compensates for local disk ephemerality.

questions.title: GKE Workload Identity
questions.scenario: Your GKE pods need to access Cloud Storage buckets securely without embedding service account keys in the application.
questions.questionText: What is the recommended way to authenticate GKE workloads to Google Cloud services?

choices.text: Service account key files mounted as secrets
Node service account shared by all pods
Application Default Credentials with user credentials

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The recommended authentication method for GKE workloads binds Kubernetes service accounts to GCP IAM service accounts, providing automatic short-lived credential rotation without any key files to manage.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Workload Identity is Google's recommended way for GKE pods to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs. It creates a binding between a Kubernetes service account and a GCP IAM service account, so pods automatically receive short-lived, auto-rotating tokens without any key files. Service account key files (B) create security risks because they are long-lived credentials that can be leaked or stolen. Node service accounts (C) grant overly broad access since all pods on a node share the same identity. User credentials (D) violate the principle of using service accounts for workloads. Workload Identity provides the most secure, least-privilege authentication model.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Workload Identity Federation for GKE extends this model to non-GCP Kubernetes clusters (EKS, AKS, on-prem), allowing external workloads to authenticate to GCP APIs without service account keys by federating trust through OIDC providers.
  • Workload Identity is enabled by default on GKE Autopilot clusters; on Standard clusters, you must enable it at the cluster level and configure the Kubernetes-to-GCP service account binding using IAM policy bindings with the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role.
  • Without Workload Identity, the default behavior is for all pods on a node to inherit the node's GCE service account, which typically has Project Editor permissions, creating a massive blast radius if any pod is compromised.
  • Workload Identity integrates with GKE's metadata server to intercept calls to the GCE metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), returning pod-specific credentials instead of the node's service account credentials, ensuring per-pod identity isolation.

questions.title: GKE Network Policies
questions.scenario: You need to restrict network traffic between pods in your GKE cluster so that only the frontend pods can communicate with the backend pods.
questions.questionText: What should you implement to control pod-to-pod network traffic?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Pod-level network segmentation within a Kubernetes cluster is enforced by declaring policies that use label selectors to specify which pods can communicate with each other over which ports.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Kubernetes Network Policies specify how groups of pods are allowed to communicate with each other and with external endpoints. They use label selectors to identify source and destination pods, defining ingress and egress rules at the pod level. VPC firewall rules (B) operate at the VM/node level and cannot distinguish between individual pods on the same node. Cloud Armor (C) protects external-facing services from DDoS and web attacks, not internal pod-to-pod traffic. IAM permissions (D) control API access to GCP resources, not network-layer pod communication. In GKE, network policies require enabling a network policy provider: either Calico or GKE Dataplane V2.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GKE Dataplane V2 (powered by Cilium and eBPF) provides native, high-performance network policy enforcement without the overhead of iptables-based solutions like Calico, and adds built-in network policy logging for audit compliance.
  • By default, Kubernetes allows all pod-to-pod communication within a cluster (flat network model); once you apply any NetworkPolicy to a namespace, pods in that namespace with matching labels begin enforcing the policy, and unmatched traffic is denied.
  • VPC firewall rules apply at the node (VM) level using IP ranges and tags, so they cannot selectively allow frontend-pod-to-backend-pod traffic when both pod types may run on the same node, making them insufficient for fine-grained pod-level segmentation.
  • For defense-in-depth, combine Kubernetes Network Policies (pod-level) with VPC firewall rules (node-level) and Cloud Armor (edge-level) to create layered network security covering internal traffic, node-to-node traffic, and external-facing traffic respectively.

questions.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
questions.scenario: Your GKE deployment needs to automatically scale the number of pods based on CPU utilization, maintaining 70% average utilization.
questions.questionText: Which Kubernetes resource automatically scales pod replicas based on metrics?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The Kubernetes resource that automatically adjusts the number of pod replicas in a deployment based on observed metrics like CPU utilization scales horizontally by adding or removing pod instances.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automatically scales the number of pod replicas in a deployment, replica set, or stateful set based on observed CPU, memory, or custom metrics. You define a target utilization (e.g., 70% CPU), and HPA adjusts replica count to maintain that target. Cluster Autoscaler (A) scales nodes, not pods. Vertical Pod Autoscaler (C) adjusts per-pod resource requests and limits, not replica count. Node Auto-provisioner (D) creates new node pools based on scheduling needs. HPA and Cluster Autoscaler work together: HPA adds pods, and if nodes are full, the Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes to accommodate the new pods.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• HPA can scale based on multiple metrics simultaneously (CPU, memory, custom Prometheus metrics, Cloud Monitoring metrics); when multiple metrics are configured, HPA calculates the desired replica count for each and uses the highest value.
  • Custom metrics from Cloud Monitoring (e.g., Pub/Sub subscription backlog, application-specific queue depth, request latency percentiles) can drive HPA scaling via the Custom Metrics Stackdriver Adapter, enabling business-logic-aware autoscaling.
  • Do not use HPA and VPA on the same metric for the same deployment: HPA adds pods to handle load while VPA resizes existing pods, and both adjusting the same metric creates conflicting scaling decisions and oscillation.
  • HPA v2 supports scaling policies that control the rate of scale-up and scale-down (e.g., add at most 4 pods per 60 seconds, remove at most 10% of pods per 5 minutes), preventing aggressive scaling oscillations during traffic fluctuations.

questions.title: Vertical Pod Autoscaler
questions.scenario: Your pods were initially configured with resource requests that don't match actual usage. You want to automatically adjust CPU and memory requests based on actual consumption.
questions.questionText: Which GKE feature automatically adjusts pod resource requests based on usage?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The GKE feature that analyzes actual pod resource consumption over time and recommends or automatically updates the CPU and memory requests for each pod scales vertically rather than horizontally.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) analyzes historical pod CPU and memory usage and either recommends or automatically adjusts resource requests to match actual consumption. HPA (A) scales the number of pod replicas, not individual pod resources. Pod Disruption Budgets (C) control how many pods can be unavailable during voluntary disruptions like upgrades. Limit Ranges (D) set default and maximum resource constraints per namespace but do not dynamically adjust based on usage. VPA is essential for right-sizing pods that were initially configured with guessed resource requests, reducing waste from over-provisioning and preventing OOM kills from under-provisioning.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• VPA operates in three modes: Off (generates recommendations only, no changes applied), Initial (sets resource requests only when pods are first created, does not update running pods), and Auto (evicts and recreates pods with updated resource requests when significant changes are needed).
  • In Auto mode, VPA must restart pods to apply new resource values because Kubernetes does not support in-place resource updates for running pods; this means VPA-managed workloads should have multiple replicas or tolerant update policies to maintain availability during restarts.
  • Never use VPA and HPA on the same metric (e.g., both targeting CPU) for the same workload because HPA tries to maintain a utilization target by adjusting replica count while VPA tries to match requests to actual usage, creating conflicting and oscillating scaling decisions.
  • VPA recommendations can be exported to a CI/CD pipeline for review before applying, using the Off mode as a recommendation engine that feeds into infrastructure-as-code reviews rather than making autonomous changes to production workloads.

questions.title: Choosing Between Compute Options
questions.scenario: A developer wants to run a simple Python script that processes uploaded files. They want minimal infrastructure management and fast deployment.
questions.questionText: Which service requires the least operational overhead for running event-driven code?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The service with the absolute lowest operational overhead lets you deploy just your function code with zero infrastructure configuration: no VMs, no containers, no clusters, no app configuration files.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Functions has the lowest operational overhead among all GCP compute options: deploy only your function code, and GCP handles all infrastructure, scaling, and runtime management. Compute Engine (B) requires provisioning, patching, and managing VMs. GKE Standard (C) requires managing Kubernetes clusters, node pools, and container orchestration. App Engine flexible (D) requires managing app.yaml configuration, Dockerfiles, and incurs instance-based pricing with minimum running instances. For a simple event-driven Python script triggered by file uploads, Cloud Functions delivers the fastest path from code to production with pay-per-invocation pricing.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Functions 2nd gen (built on Cloud Run) supports traffic splitting for A/B testing, concurrency for better resource utilization, and longer timeouts (60 min), making it suitable for more complex event-driven workloads beyond simple scripts.
  • For applications that outgrow Cloud Functions constraints (need custom runtimes, longer execution, gRPC, or WebSockets), Cloud Run is the natural next step, offering container flexibility while retaining serverless operational simplicity.
  • App Engine flexible environment requires managing an app.yaml deployment descriptor, runs on full Compute Engine VMs with instance-based pricing, and has minimum one running instance, making its operational overhead significantly higher than Cloud Functions.
  • Decision tree for GCP serverless: Cloud Functions for simple event handlers and lightweight APIs; Cloud Run for containerized applications with custom dependencies; App Engine for traditional web apps wanting managed versioning and traffic splitting without containerization.

questions.title: Sole-Tenant Nodes
questions.scenario: Your company has licensing requirements that mandate physical separation of workloads from other customers' VMs.
questions.questionText: Which Compute Engine feature provides dedicated physical servers for your VMs only?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When compliance or licensing requires that your VMs run on physical servers not shared with any other customer, you need dedicated hardware that is exclusively reserved for your project.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Sole-tenant nodes are physical Compute Engine servers dedicated exclusively to your project's workloads, ensuring no other customer's VMs share the same hardware. Preemptible VMs (A) are cost-optimized interruptible instances on shared infrastructure. Committed use discounts (B) are a pricing mechanism, not a hardware isolation feature. Custom machine types (C) allow flexible vCPU/memory configurations but still run on shared multi-tenant hardware. Sole-tenant nodes address compliance requirements for physical isolation (HIPAA, PCI-DSS), bring-your-own-license (BYOL) scenarios for per-core or per-processor licensed software, and workloads that cannot coexist with other tenants.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Node templates define the server type and configuration; node groups manage a set of sole-tenant nodes with autoscaling policies that add or remove physical servers based on VM scheduling demand.
  • Use node affinity labels and anti-affinity rules to control exactly which VMs land on which sole-tenant nodes, enabling workload segregation (e.g., production vs development) within your dedicated hardware fleet.
  • Sole-tenant nodes support Windows Server BYOL with automatic license tracking, allowing you to use existing per-core Windows licenses on dedicated hardware instead of paying the premium for GCP-licensed Windows images.
  • Sole-tenant node pricing is per-node (you pay for the entire physical server regardless of how many VMs you place on it), so maximize utilization by bin-packing multiple VMs onto each node to achieve cost efficiency comparable to multi-tenant instances.

questions.title: Live Migration
questions.scenario: Google needs to perform maintenance on the physical host running your VM. You need to ensure your application remains available during this maintenance.
questions.questionText: Which Compute Engine feature moves VMs between hosts without downtime during maintenance?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Compute Engine can transparently move a running VM from one physical host to another during maintenance events without stopping the VM or interrupting your application.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Live migration allows Compute Engine to transparently move a running VM from one physical host to another without stopping or rebooting it, ensuring near-zero downtime during host maintenance events. Snapshot restore (A) requires stopping the VM, creating a snapshot, and restoring to a new instance. Instance clone (B) creates a copy but does not transparently move the running state. Manual failover (D) requires application-level logic and introduces downtime. Live migration is the default on-host-maintenance behavior for most VM types, and Google initiates it automatically during scheduled maintenance with no user action required.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• VMs with GPUs or local SSDs cannot be live migrated due to hardware state that cannot be transferred between hosts; these VMs must be configured with on-host-maintenance set to TERMINATE, with automatic-restart enabled to recover on a healthy host.
  • The on-host-maintenance setting offers two options: MIGRATE (live migration, the default) and TERMINATE (stop the VM); choose TERMINATE only for workloads that cannot tolerate the brief network latency variation during migration or that use non-migratable hardware.
  • During live migration, the VM's memory state, CPU registers, and network connections are incrementally transferred to the destination host; applications may experience a brief pause (typically under 1 second) during the final cutover, with slightly elevated network latency during the transfer.
  • Live migration is a key differentiator of Google Cloud: it enables Google to patch, update, and maintain host hardware without requiring customers to schedule maintenance windows or tolerate downtime, supporting 99.99% availability SLAs for regional configurations.

questions.title: Cloud Run Jobs
questions.scenario: You need to run a batch data processing task that executes to completion and then exits. The task should not respond to HTTP requests.
questions.questionText: Which Cloud Run feature is designed for batch workloads that run to completion?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Run offers a workload type specifically designed for batch containers that execute their task and exit, without needing to listen for incoming HTTP requests or maintain a persistent server process.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Run jobs run containers that perform work and exit upon completion, unlike Cloud Run services which listen for and respond to incoming HTTP/gRPC requests. Jobs are ideal for batch data processing, ETL pipelines, database migrations, and scheduled maintenance tasks. Cloud Run services (B) are designed for long-running request-serving workloads. Cloud Functions HTTP trigger (C) requires listening for HTTP requests and has shorter timeout limits for 1st gen. Cloud Scheduler (D) is a cron-like trigger mechanism that can invoke jobs but is not a compute execution environment itself. Jobs support parallel task execution and automatic retry on failure.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Run jobs can be triggered manually via Console/CLI, programmatically via the Cloud Run Admin API, or on a schedule via Cloud Scheduler, which sends an HTTP request to the Cloud Run jobs API to start an execution.
  • Configure task count (1 to 10,000) for parallelism: each task runs as an independent container instance with a unique CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX environment variable, enabling embarrassingly parallel processing patterns like MapReduce-style workloads.
  • Jobs support the same container configurations as services (CPU up to 8 vCPUs, memory up to 32 GiB, Secret Manager integration, VPC connector for private networking), with timeout configurable up to 24 hours per task for long-running batch processing.
  • Failed tasks are automatically retried based on configurable retry count (default 3) and backoff; use the CLOUD_RUN_TASK_ATTEMPT environment variable in your code to implement idempotent processing logic that handles retries gracefully.

questions.title: GKE Private Clusters
questions.scenario: Your security team requires that GKE nodes have no public IP addresses and are not accessible from the internet.
questions.questionText: Which GKE configuration ensures nodes are isolated from public internet access?

choices.text: Standard cluster with VPC firewall rules

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: A GKE cluster configuration exists that assigns only internal RFC 1918 IP addresses to nodes, ensuring they have no direct internet connectivity and are completely isolated from public network access.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GKE private clusters assign only internal IP addresses to nodes, ensuring they have no direct internet-facing connectivity. You can also make the control plane private, accessible only from authorized internal networks. Node network policies (A) control pod-to-pod traffic, not node internet access. VPC firewall rules (B) on a standard cluster can restrict traffic but nodes still have public IPs that could be targeted. Autopilot with default settings (D) may still use public IPs depending on configuration. Private clusters require Cloud NAT for outbound internet access (e.g., pulling container images from public registries) since nodes lack public IPs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Configure authorized networks to restrict which IP CIDR ranges can access the control plane API endpoint; in fully private mode, even the control plane has no public endpoint, and all access goes through Private Service Connect or VPC peering.
  • Private Service Connect provides a private endpoint for the GKE control plane within your VPC, eliminating the need for VPC peering and providing a more scalable and secure connectivity model for large-scale deployments.
  • Nodes in private clusters need Cloud NAT configured on the VPC subnet to pull container images from public registries (Docker Hub, gcr.io, ghcr.io); alternatively, mirror required images to Artifact Registry to eliminate external registry dependencies entirely.
  • Private clusters pair well with VPC Service Controls to create a security perimeter around GCP resources, preventing data exfiltration even if a pod is compromised, by restricting which GCP APIs can be called from within the perimeter.

questions.title: VM Startup Scripts
questions.scenario: You need to automatically install software and configure settings when a new VM instance starts.
questions.questionText: How can you automatically run commands when a Compute Engine VM starts?

choices.text: Manually SSH and run commands after each start
Use Cloud Build to modify running VMs
Use a startup script in VM metadata

hints.label: Brief Hint
