hints.content: Compute Engine supports placing a script in the VM's metadata that runs automatically every time the instance boots, enabling hands-free software installation and configuration.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Compute Engine VMs support startup scripts specified in instance metadata, which execute automatically each time the VM starts or restarts. You can provide the script inline as metadata or reference a script URL stored in Cloud Storage. Manually SSHing after each start (B) is error-prone and unscalable. Cloud Build (C) is a CI/CD service for building artifacts, not for configuring running VMs. Option D is factually incorrect. Startup scripts are essential for bootstrapping VMs in managed instance groups where new instances are created automatically by the autoscaler or autohealer and must configure themselves without manual intervention.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Linux VMs use the startup-script metadata key for inline scripts or startup-script-url to reference a script in Cloud Storage; the script runs as root during the boot process after networking is available.
  • Windows VMs use windows-startup-script-ps1 for PowerShell scripts or windows-startup-script-bat for batch files, with equivalent URL variants for Cloud Storage-hosted scripts.
  • Shutdown scripts (shutdown-script metadata key) run when a VM is stopped or preempted, providing a window to save state, flush caches, or deregister from service discovery before termination completes.
  • For complex or lengthy configurations, prefer baking software into custom images (reducing boot time and external dependencies) and using startup scripts only for dynamic configuration like fetching secrets, registering with a service mesh, or joining a cluster.

questions.title: Spot VM Limitations
questions.scenario: You're considering Spot VMs for a production web server that must maintain 99.9% availability.
questions.questionText: Why are Spot VMs NOT recommended for this production web server?

choices.text: Spot VMs are more expensive than standard VMs
Spot VMs have lower network performance
Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with 30-second warning
Spot VMs cannot use load balancers

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The fundamental limitation of Spot VMs is that Google can reclaim them at any moment with only 30 seconds of warning, making them incompatible with workloads that require guaranteed uptime or high availability SLAs.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Spot VMs can be preempted by Google at any time when compute capacity is needed, providing only a 30-second ACPI G2 shutdown signal before termination. This makes them fundamentally unsuitable for production web servers requiring 99.9% availability (less than 8.76 hours downtime per year). Option A is wrong because Spot VMs are 60-91% cheaper. Option C is incorrect because Spot VMs fully support load balancers. Option D is false because Spot VMs have identical network performance to standard VMs of the same machine type. The preemption risk directly conflicts with the high-availability requirement stated in the scenario.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Spot VMs carry no SLA whatsoever; Google provides no guarantee on availability, and preemption rates vary significantly by zone, region, and machine type, sometimes exceeding 50% in popular configurations during peak demand periods.
  • For production web servers requiring high availability, use standard on-demand VMs with committed use discounts (CUDs) for cost savings: 3-year CUDs offer up to 70% discount with guaranteed capacity, nearly matching Spot savings without preemption risk.
  • Spot VMs can be strategically mixed with on-demand VMs in managed instance groups for non-critical burst capacity: configure the MIG to prefer Spot VMs up to a percentage, falling back to on-demand when Spot capacity is unavailable.
  • The 30-second preemption notice is delivered as a metadata attribute change and an ACPI G2 soft-off signal; applications that need graceful shutdown must handle this signal by completing in-flight requests, draining connections, and saving state within that narrow window.

questions.title: Container-Optimized OS
questions.scenario: You need to run containers on Compute Engine with a minimal, secure, and auto-updating operating system.
questions.questionText: Which OS image is optimized for running containers on Compute Engine?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Google maintains a purpose-built, minimal operating system designed exclusively for running containers, featuring a locked-down filesystem, automatic security updates, and Docker pre-installed out of the box.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Container-Optimized OS (COS) is a Google-maintained, Chromium OS-based operating system specifically designed for running containers on Compute Engine. It features a minimal attack surface, a read-only root filesystem, automatic security updates, and Docker/containerd pre-installed. CentOS (A) and Ubuntu (B) are general-purpose Linux distributions with larger attack surfaces and more manual configuration needed for container workloads. Windows Server with containers (D) carries significant overhead and is designed for Windows container workloads only. GKE uses COS as the default node image, validating its production readiness for container workloads at scale.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• COS images are based on Chromium OS and receive automatic over-the-air security updates from Google, patching vulnerabilities without requiring manual intervention or scheduled maintenance windows.
  • The root filesystem is mounted read-only, preventing persistent modifications by malware or misconfigurations; writable areas are limited to /home, /var, and /tmp, with container data stored in designated data partitions.
  • COS includes only the minimum packages needed to run containers (kernel, container runtime, cloud-init), omitting package managers like apt or yum; use cloud-init or startup scripts with docker run commands to deploy your containerized applications.
  • Two COS variants exist: cos (Docker-based, legacy) and cos-containerd (containerd-based, used by GKE by default); cos-containerd is recommended for new deployments as it aligns with the Kubernetes ecosystem's move away from Docker as a runtime.

questions.title: Cloud Run Traffic Splitting
questions.scenario: You want to gradually roll out a new version of your Cloud Run service, sending 10% of traffic to the new revision while monitoring for errors.
questions.questionText: Which Cloud Run feature enables gradual rollouts between revisions?

choices.text: Cloud Run does not support canary deployments
Multiple Cloud Run services behind a load balancer

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Run natively supports splitting traffic by percentage across multiple revisions of the same service, enabling canary deployments and gradual rollouts without any external load balancer configuration.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Run has built-in traffic splitting that allows you to route specified percentages of traffic to different revisions of the same service. This enables canary deployments (e.g., 10% to the new version), A/B testing, and gradual rollouts without needing external load balancers or DNS changes. Option A is factually wrong since traffic splitting is a core Cloud Run feature. Multiple services behind a load balancer (B) adds unnecessary complexity. Manual DNS switching (D) does not allow percentage-based gradual rollout. You can also assign unique URLs to revisions via tags for direct testing before routing any production traffic.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Each Cloud Run revision can receive a unique URL via revision tags (e.g., https://canary---myservice-xyz.a.run.app), allowing direct testing of new revisions by developers or QA before any production traffic is routed to them.
  • Traffic splitting can be automated in CI/CD pipelines using Cloud Deploy, which orchestrates progressive delivery with configurable canary percentages, verification steps, and automatic rollback on failure detection.
  • Rollback is instantaneous: shift 100% of traffic back to the previous stable revision with a single gcloud run services update-traffic command, with no container restart or redeployment needed since both revisions remain running.
  • Cloud Run maintains old revisions until explicitly deleted or garbage-collected, and revisions scaled to zero incur no compute charges, so keeping multiple revisions available for quick rollback has minimal cost impact.

questions.title: Shielded VMs
questions.scenario: Your security policy requires protection against rootkits and boot-level malware on all VMs.
questions.questionText: Which Compute Engine feature provides verified boot integrity and protection against boot-level threats?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The Compute Engine security feature that verifies the integrity of the boot process using Secure Boot, a virtual TPM, and integrity monitoring protects against rootkits and boot-level malware before the OS loads.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Shielded VMs provide verifiable integrity of the VM boot process through three mechanisms: Secure Boot (ensures only signed bootloaders and kernels execute), vTPM (virtual Trusted Platform Module for measured boot and key storage), and integrity monitoring (compares boot measurements against a known-good baseline). Custom images (A) are disk images without boot verification capabilities. Sole-tenant nodes (C) provide physical hardware isolation but do not verify boot integrity. Confidential VMs (D) encrypt data in memory but address a different threat model than boot-level attacks. Shielded VMs are specifically designed to detect and prevent rootkits, bootkits, and kernel-level malware.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Secure Boot validates the digital signatures of all boot components (UEFI firmware, bootloader, kernel) against certificates stored in the VM's UEFI Secure Boot database, refusing to boot if any component has been tampered with or is unsigned.
  • The vTPM (virtual Trusted Platform Module) performs measured boot by recording hashes of each boot stage in Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs), and can be used by applications for disk encryption key sealing and remote attestation workflows.
  • Integrity monitoring uses Cloud Logging to track boot measurement changes between boots, alerting you via Cloud Monitoring if the boot sequence deviates from the established baseline, which could indicate a compromised kernel or bootloader.
  • Shielded VMs can be combined with Confidential VMs (memory encryption) and sole-tenant nodes (physical isolation) for defense-in-depth: boot integrity plus runtime memory protection plus hardware-level tenant isolation.

questions.title: Confidential VMs
questions.scenario: You need to process sensitive data and require encryption of data in memory, protecting it even from the hypervisor.
questions.questionText: Which Compute Engine feature encrypts data while it's being processed in memory?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Confidential computing uses hardware-based memory encryption so that data remains encrypted even while being actively processed in RAM, protecting it from the cloud provider's infrastructure and other tenants.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Confidential VMs use hardware-based memory encryption (AMD SEV or Intel TDX) to encrypt data while it is being processed in memory, protecting it from the cloud provider, hypervisor, and other VMs on the same host. Customer-managed encryption keys (A) control encryption of data at rest on disks, not in-memory data. Shielded VMs (B) verify boot integrity but do not encrypt memory contents. Private Google Access (D) enables VMs without public IPs to reach Google APIs, unrelated to data encryption. Confidential VMs address the "data in use" protection gap, completing the encryption triad of data at rest, in transit, and in use.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Confidential VMs are available on N2D machine types (using AMD SEV, Secure Encrypted Virtualization) and C3 machine types (using Intel TDX, Trust Domain Extensions), with each technology providing hardware-enforced memory isolation at the processor level.
  • AMD SEV encrypts each VM's memory with a unique encryption key managed by a dedicated secure processor on the AMD CPU, making it cryptographically impossible for the hypervisor or other VMs to read the VM's memory contents.
  • Confidential GKE nodes extend this protection to Kubernetes workloads: enable Confidential Computing on a node pool to ensure all pods running on those nodes have hardware-encrypted memory, transparent to the application code.
  • Combine Confidential VMs with CMEK (Customer-Managed Encryption Keys) for data at rest, VPC encryption for data in transit, and Shielded VMs for boot integrity to achieve comprehensive encryption coverage across all data states.

questions.title: MIG Rolling Updates
questions.scenario: You need to update all VMs in a managed instance group to a new instance template with zero downtime.
questions.questionText: How should you update VMs in a MIG with minimal disruption?

choices.text: Manually update each VM one at a time
Use rolling update with maxSurge and maxUnavailable settings
Delete and recreate the entire MIG
MIGs do not support updates after creation

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: MIGs support rolling updates that gradually replace instances with new ones based on a new instance template, using configurable parameters to control how many extra or unavailable instances are allowed during the transition.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: MIG rolling updates gradually replace instances with ones created from the updated instance template. You configure maxSurge (the number of extra instances created above the target size during the update) and maxUnavailable (the number of instances that can be offline simultaneously). Manually updating each VM (A) is error-prone and does not scale. Deleting and recreating the entire MIG (C) causes full downtime. Option D is factually incorrect. For zero downtime, set maxSurge to 1+ (create new instances before removing old ones) and maxUnavailable to 0 (never reduce capacity below the target size during the update).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Two update types exist: proactive (immediately starts replacing instances to match the new template) and opportunistic (waits for instances to be recreated by other events like autohealing or manual restarts before applying the new template).
  • Canary updates allow you to apply the new template to a small subset of instances first (e.g., 20%) to validate the new configuration before proceeding with a full rollout, reducing the blast radius of configuration errors.
  • Rollback by initiating a new rolling update that points back to the previous instance template; the MIG uses the same maxSurge/maxUnavailable parameters to gradually replace the new instances with ones matching the old template.
  • Configure health check-based verification during rolling updates: the MIG waits for each new instance to pass health checks before considering it healthy and proceeding to replace the next batch, preventing cascading failures from a broken template.

questions.title: App Engine Traffic Management
questions.scenario: You have deployed a new version of your App Engine application and want to gradually migrate traffic from the old version.
questions.questionText: How can you control traffic distribution between App Engine versions?

choices.text: App Engine only supports instant cutover
Deploy to a different project for testing
Use traffic splitting to distribute traffic by percentage

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: App Engine has built-in traffic splitting that lets you distribute traffic between multiple deployed versions by percentage, enabling gradual migrations and canary deployments without any external infrastructure.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: App Engine traffic splitting allows you to distribute incoming traffic between multiple deployed versions by specifying a percentage for each version. You can split traffic by IP address (consistent routing for each user), by cookie (more accurate session affinity), or randomly (even distribution). Option B is wrong because App Engine explicitly supports gradual traffic migration. Deploying to a different project (C) makes traffic splitting impossible without external routing. An external load balancer (D) is unnecessary because App Engine provides this capability natively. Traffic splitting is controlled via the Cloud Console, gcloud CLI, or the Admin API.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• IP-based splitting uses the hash of the client IP to route consistently to the same version, but is less accurate when users share IPs (corporate proxies, NAT); cookie-based splitting uses the GOOGAPPUID cookie for precise per-user version affinity.
  • Each App Engine version has a unique URL (VERSION-dot-SERVICE-dot-PROJECT.appspot.com) for direct testing before routing any production traffic, allowing QA validation of the new version without affecting live users.
  • App Engine supports gradual traffic migration that automatically ramps traffic to the new version over a configurable period, or manual migration where you control the exact percentage at each step of the rollout.
  • Traffic splitting operates at the App Engine service level (not project level), so each service (e.g., default, api, worker) can independently manage its own version rollout cadence and traffic distribution strategy.

questions.title: GKE Release Channels
questions.scenario: Your team wants automatic Kubernetes version upgrades while maintaining stability for production workloads.
questions.questionText: Which GKE feature provides managed version upgrades with different stability levels?

choices.text: GKE does not support automatic upgrades
Automatic upgrade to latest version immediately

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GKE offers multiple release channels that provide automatic Kubernetes version upgrades at different velocities, letting you choose between early access to new features and maximum production stability.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GKE release channels (Rapid, Regular, Stable) provide automatic, managed Kubernetes version upgrades with different maturity levels. Rapid receives new versions first for early testing, Regular provides a balanced approach for most workloads, and Stable offers the most-tested versions with the longest validation period. Option A is false because automatic upgrades are a core GKE capability. Manual version pinning (B) is possible but is not a managed upgrade feature. Option D is incorrect because upgrades are staged through channels, not applied immediately to all clusters. Channels ensure your cluster stays on supported, security-patched versions without manual intervention.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• An Extended channel is available for customers with premium support, providing even longer support windows for stable versions, giving teams more time to validate and prepare for Kubernetes minor version upgrades.
  • Maintenance windows and maintenance exclusions control exactly when automatic upgrades occur (e.g., only during off-peak hours on weekdays) and when they are blocked (e.g., during holiday freezes), giving you operational control within the automated upgrade framework.
  • Surge upgrades minimize disruption during node pool upgrades by creating additional nodes (surge nodes) before draining and upgrading existing nodes, ensuring workload capacity is maintained throughout the upgrade process.
  • Node auto-upgrade (enabled by default with release channels) automatically upgrades nodes to match the control plane version, with configurable blue-green or surge strategies and respect for pod disruption budgets to maintain application availability.

questions.title: VM Scheduling Options
questions.scenario: You have development VMs that are only needed during business hours and should be stopped overnight to save costs.
questions.questionText: What is the best way to automatically stop VMs on a schedule?

choices.text: Use Spot VMs which stop automatically
Scheduled VM management is not supported
Use instance schedules to start/stop VMs automatically

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Compute Engine provides native instance schedule resources that automatically start and stop VMs based on a defined time-based schedule, eliminating the need for manual intervention or external automation tools.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Compute Engine instance schedules automatically start and stop VMs based on a configured time schedule, making them ideal for dev/test environments that should run only during business hours. Spot VMs (A) are preempted based on capacity needs, not on a predictable schedule. Manual stopping (B) is error-prone, unscalable, and easily forgotten. Option D is factually incorrect. Instance schedules use IANA timezone-aware scheduling to ensure VMs start and stop at the correct local times regardless of daylight saving changes, and they can be attached to individual VMs or applied across multiple instances via instance templates.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Instance schedules are standalone resources created with start and stop times in cron-like format; you attach them to VM instances, and the Compute Engine service automatically executes the start/stop operations at the specified times.
  • An alternative approach uses Cloud Scheduler (cron) triggering a Cloud Function that calls the Compute Engine API to start/stop VMs, offering more flexibility for complex logic (e.g., skip holidays, check for active SSH sessions) but requiring more setup and maintenance.
  • Stopped VMs incur no compute charges (vCPU, memory), but persistent disks, static external IPs, and any attached licenses continue to be billed; to fully eliminate costs, also consider using ephemeral IPs and deleting unused disks.
  • For development environments, combine instance schedules with committed use discounts carefully: CUDs commit to minimum resource usage regardless of whether VMs are running, so stopping dev VMs overnight does not reduce CUD charges. Use on-demand pricing for scheduled dev workloads.

questions.title: Cloud Functions 2nd Generation
questions.scenario: Your function needs to run for longer than 9 minutes and requires more memory than 1st generation supports.
questions.questionText: Which Cloud Functions version supports longer timeouts and more resources?

choices.text: Cloud Functions 1st generation with extended timeout
Cloud Functions does not support long-running tasks

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The newer generation of Cloud Functions is built on Cloud Run infrastructure, significantly expanding resource limits including timeout duration up to 60 minutes and memory allocation up to 32 GiB.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Functions 2nd generation is built on Cloud Run infrastructure and substantially increases resource limits compared to 1st gen: timeouts up to 60 minutes (vs 9 minutes), memory up to 32 GiB (vs 8 GiB), and up to 8 vCPUs. Option A is wrong because the generations have very different limits. Option B is incorrect because 1st gen does not support extended timeouts beyond 9 minutes. Option D is false because 2nd gen supports long-running tasks. Additionally, 2nd gen adds concurrency support (multiple requests per instance), traffic splitting for canary testing, and Eventarc-based triggers supporting 90+ event sources.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• 2nd gen supports configurable concurrency (up to 1000 concurrent requests per instance), dramatically improving resource efficiency for I/O-bound functions by amortizing cold start and memory overhead across multiple simultaneous requests.
  • Eventarc integration enables 2nd gen functions to trigger from 90+ event sources including Cloud Audit Logs, allowing you to react to virtually any GCP API action (e.g., a new BigQuery table created, a Pub/Sub topic modified, a VM started).
  • 2nd gen functions can use minimum instances to keep warm containers ready, reducing cold start latency identically to Cloud Run's minimum instances feature, since 2nd gen functions are Cloud Run services under the hood.
  • Migration from 1st gen to 2nd gen requires updating the function signature (using CloudEvent format for event triggers instead of the legacy background function format) and redeploying, but the deployment workflow and gcloud commands remain similar.

questions.title: Artifact Registry for Containers
questions.scenario: You need a secure, private registry to store container images used by your GKE clusters and Cloud Run services.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides a managed container registry integrated with GKE and Cloud Run?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP's current recommended service for storing and managing container images is a universal artifact management platform that also supports language packages and integrates natively with GKE, Cloud Run, and Cloud Build.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Artifact Registry is Google Cloud's universal artifact management service and the recommended replacement for the deprecated Container Registry. It stores Docker container images, Helm charts, and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, Go), integrates with Cloud Build for CI/CD, GKE and Cloud Run for deployment, and provides vulnerability scanning. Cloud Source Repositories (A) stores source code, not container images. Cloud Storage (B) is object storage, not a container registry. Container Registry (C) is deprecated and being sunset in favor of Artifact Registry, which offers superior features including IAM-based access control, regional and multi-regional repositories, and cross-format artifact storage.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Container Registry (gcr.io) is deprecated; Google recommends migrating to Artifact Registry, which provides the same Docker V2 API compatibility plus fine-grained IAM permissions at the repository level (instead of the bucket-level permissions gcr.io used).
  • Artifact Registry supports multiple artifact formats in a single service: Docker images, Helm charts, Maven/Gradle packages, npm packages, Python packages, Go modules, and APT/YUM OS packages, consolidating artifact management.
  • Binary Authorization integrates with Artifact Registry to enforce deploy-time policies: only container images that have been signed (attested) by trusted authorities can be deployed to GKE or Cloud Run, preventing unauthorized or unscanned images from reaching production.
  • Artifact Registry provides automatic vulnerability scanning powered by Container Analysis, which checks images against known CVE databases and can block deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities when combined with Binary Authorization policies.

questions.title: OS Patch Management
questions.scenario: You need to ensure all Compute Engine VMs are patched with the latest security updates and maintain compliance reports.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service manages OS patch deployment and compliance for Compute Engine VMs?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP provides a centralized fleet management service that automates OS patch deployment across Compute Engine VMs, tracks patch compliance status, and generates reports for security audits.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: VM Manager (which includes OS Patch Management) automates OS patch deployment across your Compute Engine VM fleet, provides compliance reporting, and supports scheduled patch jobs for both Windows and Linux VMs. Manual SSH patching (A) does not scale and cannot provide compliance reports. Cloud Build (B) is a CI/CD service for building and testing code, not for OS-level patching. Deployment Manager (C) provisions infrastructure but does not manage ongoing OS patches. VM Manager reduces the security risk window by automating the patch lifecycle and providing visibility into which VMs are out of compliance with your patching policies.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The OS Config agent must be installed on each VM (it comes pre-installed on most Google-provided public images); it communicates with the VM Manager service to receive patch jobs, report inventory, and execute compliance policies.
  • Patch jobs can be scoped using filters (by zone, label, instance name, or OS type) and configured with rollout settings (percentage-based or zone-by-zone) to control the blast radius and avoid patching all VMs simultaneously.
  • OS Inventory management tracks all installed packages, available updates, and Windows Update/apt/yum repository metadata across your fleet, providing a centralized view of your VM software inventory for compliance auditing and vulnerability assessment.
  • OS Policies (declarative configuration management) extend VM Manager beyond patching to enforce desired state: ensure specific packages are installed, files exist with expected content, or scripts have run successfully, similar to lightweight configuration management without external tools.

questions.title: Compute Service Selection
questions.scenario: A company needs to choose the right GCP compute service for different workloads: a stateless API, a legacy monolithic application requiring specific OS configurations, and a machine learning training pipeline.
questions.questionText: What is the best mapping of workloads to compute services?

choices.text: App Engine for all three workloads
Cloud Run for stateless API, Compute Engine for legacy app, Vertex AI with GPUs for ML training
Cloud Functions for all three workloads

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The best practice for GCP compute selection is matching each workload to the service that best fits its specific requirements: serverless for stateless APIs, VMs for legacy apps needing OS control, and specialized ML platforms for training pipelines.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Each workload maps to the compute service best suited for its requirements. Cloud Run handles the stateless API with automatic scaling, pay-per-use pricing, and zero server management. Compute Engine provides the full VM control and specific OS configurations the legacy monolith needs. Vertex AI with GPU/TPU support (or Compute Engine with GPUs) is purpose-built for ML training pipelines. App Engine for all three (B) cannot handle specific OS requirements or ML training efficiently. GKE for all three (C) adds unnecessary Kubernetes complexity for the API and legacy app. Cloud Functions for all three (D) cannot run a monolith or ML training pipeline within its constraints.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The GCP compute decision tree considers four factors: management overhead (serverless to full-control), scaling model (event-driven, request-driven, or capacity-based), runtime requirements (language constraints, OS access, hardware accelerators), and cost model (pay-per-invocation, pay-per-request, or pay-per-resource-hour).
  • GKE is a valid choice when you need Kubernetes features (CRDs, service mesh, operators) or want to standardize on containers across diverse workloads, but it introduces significant operational complexity that should be justified by concrete Kubernetes-specific requirements.
  • Cloud Functions is best for lightweight, event-driven glue logic (file processing, webhook handlers, scheduled tasks) with execution times under 60 minutes and simple dependency trees; it should not be used as a general-purpose application runtime.
  • For ML training specifically, Vertex AI provides managed training jobs with built-in GPU/TPU support, hyperparameter tuning, experiment tracking, and integration with model serving, making it more productive than raw Compute Engine with GPUs for most ML teams.

gl-compute-engine.name: Compute Engine
gl-compute-engine.definition: GCP's Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) offering that provides virtual machines running on Google's infrastructure with full OS control.
gl-compute-engine.examNote: Compute Engine is for lift-and-shift migrations and workloads requiring full VM control.

gl-app-engine.name: App Engine
gl-app-engine.definition: A fully managed Platform as a Service (PaaS) for building and deploying web applications without managing infrastructure.
gl-app-engine.examNote: Standard environment scales to zero; flexible environment uses containers with minimum one instance.

gl-cloud-functions.name: Cloud Functions
gl-cloud-functions.definition: A serverless execution environment for building event-driven applications with automatic scaling and pay-per-use pricing.
gl-cloud-functions.examNote: 2nd generation supports longer timeouts (60 min) and is built on Cloud Run.

gl-cloud-run.name: Cloud Run
gl-cloud-run.definition: A fully managed serverless platform for running stateless containers that automatically scales based on incoming requests.
gl-cloud-run.examNote: Supports any container image; can scale to zero; built on Knative for portability.

gl-gke.name: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
gl-gke.definition: A managed Kubernetes service that provides container orchestration with automatic upgrades, scaling, and integration with GCP services.
gl-gke.examNote: Autopilot mode manages nodes and charges per pod; Standard mode gives full control over node pools.

gl-mig.name: Managed Instance Group (MIG)
gl-mig.definition: A group of identical VM instances managed as a single entity with autoscaling, autohealing, and rolling updates.
gl-mig.examNote: Regional MIGs distribute across zones for high availability; use instance templates for configuration.

gl-spot-vm.name: Spot VM
gl-spot-vm.definition: Virtual machines using excess Compute Engine capacity at 60-91% discount, which can be preempted with 30-second notice.
gl-spot-vm.examNote: Ideal for fault-tolerant batch workloads; not suitable for production services requiring high availability.

gl-cud.name: Committed Use Discount (CUD)
gl-cud.definition: A discount of up to 70% for committing to use a minimum amount of compute resources for 1 or 3 years.
gl-cud.examNote: CUDs are regional and apply across projects; best for steady-state production workloads.

gl-sud.name: Sustained Use Discount (SUD)
gl-sud.definition: Automatic discounts up to 30% applied to VMs running for more than 25% of a month, with no commitment required.
gl-sud.examNote: Applied automatically; E2 and A2 machine types do not receive SUDs.

gl-tpu.name: Tensor Processing Unit (TPU)
gl-tpu.definition: Google's custom-built ASIC designed to accelerate machine learning workloads, especially for TensorFlow and JAX models.
gl-tpu.examNote: TPU pods can scale to thousands of chips for distributed training of large models.

gl-gpu.name: Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)
gl-gpu.definition: Hardware accelerators attached to VMs for parallel processing workloads like ML training, rendering, and scientific computing.
gl-gpu.examNote: Available on N1, A2, and G2 machine types; requires driver installation.

gl-persistent-disk.name: Persistent Disk
gl-persistent-disk.definition: Durable network-attached block storage for Compute Engine VMs that persists independently of VM lifecycle.
gl-persistent-disk.examNote: Types include pd-standard, pd-balanced, pd-ssd, and pd-extreme; supports snapshots and resizing.

gl-local-ssd.name: Local SSD
gl-local-ssd.definition: High-performance, physically attached storage that provides very low latency but data is ephemeral (lost when VM stops).
gl-local-ssd.examNote: Use for caches and scratch data; cannot be detached or snapshotted.

gl-instance-template.name: Instance Template
gl-instance-template.definition: A resource that defines VM properties (machine type, disk, network, metadata) used by managed instance groups to create identical instances.
gl-instance-template.examNote: Templates are immutable; create new versions and update MIGs with rolling updates.

gl-workload-identity.name: Workload Identity
gl-workload-identity.definition: The recommended way to authenticate GKE workloads to Google Cloud APIs by linking Kubernetes service accounts to GCP IAM service accounts.
gl-workload-identity.examNote: Eliminates need for service account keys; provides automatic credential rotation.
